Segment 0

Where do we even start?

The question

We can measure how wrong the model is. Is that enough to make it better?

One number. One guess. Nothing else to go on.

A delivery service wants to predict how long a delivery takes from how far it has to go. One number to learn: minutes per kilometre.

python
# ---- the model -------------------------------------------------------
# One parameter, w, the minutes each kilometre costs us.
def predict(w, distance_km):
    return w * distance_km

# ---- the score -------------------------------------------------------
# Mean squared error. For every delivery: take the prediction, subtract
# the truth, and square it so that being too high and being too low are
# both counted as bad. Then average over all 200 rows.
def loss(w):
    errors = predict(w, distance_km) - delivery_time_min
    return (errors ** 2).mean()

w = 6.00                                   # our current guess
print("Current w:     %.2f" % w)
print("Current loss:  %.3f" % loss(w))     # how wrong we are right now

output

Current w:     6.00
Current loss:  28.149
Before we start · question 1

From that one score at that one value of w, can you tell whether to raise w or lower it?

The answer

No, and that is the whole problem. A single measurement tells us how high up we are, not which way the ground falls away. To get a direction we have to know something about the neighbourhood of where we stand, which means looking at more than one place.

Check yourself · question 2

We can see the whole bowl, so why not read off the lowest point and stop there?

The answer

It looks like a bowl. One bottom, and from where we stand the downhill direction is obvious. But we only drew it by scoring 561 candidates, which is a luxury we will never have again.

So from here on we use only what we can learn from where we are standing. And we still have no idea how far to move.

Segment 2

Is knowing the direction enough?

The question

Suppose someone just tells us which way is downhill. Is that enough to get to the bottom?

It sounds like it should be. One knob left: how far to step.

python
c = 2.1             # <-- the only thing we get to choose
n_steps = 200

w = 6.00
for step in range(n_steps):
    # The direction is handed to us for free. Downhill is left when the
    # slope is positive, right when it is negative.
    direction = -1 if slope_at(w) > 0 else +1

    # Always the same distance, wherever we are. This is the line that
    # is about to cause all the trouble.
    w = w + direction * c

output

after 200 steps of size 2.1:  w = 1.8000
the bottom is at w = 2.5600, so we are still 0.7600 away

c decides two things at once, and they pull opposite ways. It sets how close we end up, and it sets how long we take to get there. Big c is quick and permanently wrong. Small c is accurate and never finishes. There is no good value of c, only different bad trades.
Check yourself · question 3

With the direction always correct and a fixed step size, what happens in the end?

Check yourself · question 4

Read the table. Why is there no good value of c?

The answer

No. Knowing the direction is not enough. One number is being asked to do two jobs that pull opposite ways: it sets how close we can get, and it sets how long we take to get there.

What we actually want is a step that is big when we are far away and small when we are close. Then speed early and precision late come out of the same rule, with nothing to tune. Does anything like that already exist on this curve?

Segment 3

Is there a quantity that already knows?

The question

Is there something on this curve that is big when we are far from the bottom and small when we are close?

If there is, it can set the step size for us.

Drag the point. Watch the tangent and the panel beside it.

Segment 3 / the slope
Drag the point and watch the slope
The tangent goes navy where the slope is positive and gold where it is negative. The panel on the right runs one step of gradient descent from wherever you are holding the point.
w
loss
the derivative dLdw
one step of gradient descent
w − lr × dLdw
= − 0.30 ×
= 0
new w =
drag the point. the gold circles are fixed reference points. the bar is scaled to the steepest slope on this range, 7.84.
Watch two things as you drag. The sign flips exactly at the bottom. The size shrinks to nothing as you approach it, so out at the edges the amount subtracted is large, and near the bottom it is almost nothing.

The slope gives us both things at once, for free:

  • Its sign flips exactly at the bottom. Positive on the right side, negative on the left. That is the direction.
  • Its size shrinks to nothing as we approach the bottom and grows as we move away. That is the distance.

The slope of the loss is written dLdw and called the gradient. So subtract it, scaled by a small number lr so we do not take the whole thing at once.

w ← w − lr × dLdwThe whole algorithm. One line, and both halves of the step come from one number we can measure where we stand.
python
lr = 0.30
n_steps = 60

w = 6.00
for step in range(n_steps):
    g = gradient(w)     # the slope right here: sign AND size in one number
    w = w - lr * g      # minus, because we want to go DOWNhill
                        # far from the bottom  g is big  -> big step
                        # near the bottom      g is small -> small step

output

Check yourself · question 5

As w gets close to the bottom, what happens to the size of the gradient?

The answer

Yes. It is the slope. Its sign is the direction and its size is the distance, and the size fades out on its own as we arrive. We did not have to build that behaviour, it is just the shape of the surface we were standing on all along.

Segment 4

How big should the step multiplier be?

The question

We still have one knob: lr. What happens if we get it wrong?

Let us break it in both directions first, and only then look at a value that works.

python
# Same problem, same start, same 60 steps. Only lr changes.
for lr in [0.0201, 1.0553, 1.0050, 0.3015]:
    w = 6.00
    for step in range(60):
        w = w - lr * gradient(w)      # the one line from Segment 3
    print("lr = %.4f   w after 60 steps = %13.4f" % (lr, w))

output

lr = 0.0201   w after 60 steps =        2.8571     <-- still not there
lr = 1.0553   w after 60 steps =     1049.9766     <-- gone
lr = 1.0050   w after 60 steps =        6.0000     <-- back where it started
lr = 0.3015   w after 60 steps =        2.5600     <-- arrived

One learning rate at a time
One graph, four values of lr, picked one at a time. Same start, same 60 steps, the same single line of arithmetic. Work through them left to right: the two failures first, then the boundary between them, then a value that works.

Both ends fail, and they fail in completely different ways. Too small and it crawls. Too large and every bounce lands further out than the one before, until it is gone. So somewhere between them there is a boundary, and for this problem it sits at lr = 1.0050.

That boundary is worth a moment, because the behaviour exactly on it is the thing most people get wrong.

A change of 0.0e+00 over two hundred steps. That is rounding error in the last bits of a decimal, not progress. The loss is flat.

Now go back to the graph above and pick lr = 0.3015, the last button. That is the one you want.

Check yourself · question 7

Your loss turns into nan a few hundred steps into training. First thing to try?

Change it as you go

Put the failures together and a plan suggests itself. A big rate covers ground fast but cannot settle. A small one settles but starts far too slowly. So start big and finish small. That is a schedule, and PyTorch ships them.

python
w_param   = torch.tensor([6.00], requires_grad=True)
opt       = torch.optim.SGD([w_param], lr=0.9950)    # start just under the edge

# Halve the learning rate every 40 steps. Nothing else changes.
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(opt, step_size=40, gamma=0.5)

for step in range(200):
    opt.zero_grad()                    # clear last step's gradient
    loss = ((x * w_param - y) ** 2).mean()
    loss.backward()                    # work out the gradient
    opt.step()                         # w = w - lr * gradient
    scheduler.step()                   # and now update lr itself
    if step % 40 == 0:
        print("step %3d   lr = %.6f" % (step, scheduler.get_last_lr()[0]))

output

step   0   lr = 0.994975
step  40   lr = 0.497488
step  80   lr = 0.248744
step 120   lr = 0.124372
step 160   lr = 0.062186

Watch step 40. The run is bouncing and going nowhere, the rate halves, and it lands almost at once. That kink is the schedule doing its job.

The best possible loss is 16.37425910. Three of these reach it to the last printed digit, so the distance column is the one that separates them.

The gradient shrinks the step automatically as we approach the minimum. The learning rate schedule shrinks it a second time, on a timetable we control. In practice you need both.
Check yourself · question 8

The gradient already shrinks the step as we get close. So why add a schedule on top?

The answer

There is a window, and it is narrower than you would hope. Too small and it crawls. Past the boundary and it explodes, with no gentle warning in between. At the boundary itself the loss simply never moves.

And the best value is not one value: large is right at the start, small is right at the end. So set it large and shrink it on a timetable. In practice you use the gradient's own shrinking and a schedule.

Segment 5

How much data should one step use?

The question

Every step so far used all the data. What happens when there is too much data to use?

Two million customers, a hundred features each.

python
N_ROWS, N_FEATURES = 2_000_000, 100
X, y = load_churn(N_ROWS, N_FEATURES)


class ChurnNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1  = nn.Linear(n_features, 512)   # 100 -> 512
        self.act1 = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc2  = nn.Linear(512, 256)          # 512 -> 256
        self.act2 = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc3  = nn.Linear(256, 1)            # 256 -> one answer

    def forward(self, x):
        # Each line makes a new tensor with one row per input row, and
        # every one of them has to stay in memory until the backward pass
        # has finished with it. Remember that, it matters in a moment.
        h1 = self.act1(self.fc1(x))     # N x 512
        h2 = self.act2(self.fc2(h1))    # N x 256
        return self.fc3(h2)             # N x 1

output

feature table: (2000000, 100) float32   footprint: 0.80 GB

Use all of it, every step

The loss is an average over the whole dataset, so the correct gradient is computed over the whole dataset: all two million rows forward, one gradient, one step. This is batch gradient descent, and it is exactly right.

It is also perfectly smooth, because the gradient is the true average over every row. No sampling, no luck, no disagreement between one step and the next.

Segment 5 / stable
Batch gradient descent: use everything, every step
Every gradient here comes from all 200 rows. The path never wobbles. The right hand panel is the distance to the bottom, and it is a clean straight line down.

Worth noticing

Notice the kind of failure. Not slow, not inaccurate: impossible. The correct algorithm will not run on the hardware we own.

Use one row per step

The opposite extreme. One customer, one gradient, one step, then the next customer. This is stochastic gradient descent, and it needs about 13 kilobytes.

A single row points the right way on average, but any one customer is odd in some way, and their gradient carries that oddness along with the trend. So the path lurches.

python
for i in range(N_ROWS):
    xb = X[i:i+1]                    # exactly one row
    yb = y[i:i+1]
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = ((net(xb).squeeze(1) - yb) ** 2).mean()
    loss.backward()                  # a gradient from ONE customer, so it is
    opt.step()                       # right on average and noisy in detail

output

memory for one update: 13.1 KB

A little history

On a machine with a few megabytes of memory, batch gradient descent was not slow, it was impossible. One row at a time was not a clever idea someone had, it was the only thing that would run.

So which one is faster?

One epoch means one pass over the data, so both methods see every row exactly once.

commit to an answer before you scroll

Batch GD does ONE update per pass over the data.
SGD does 500,000 updates per pass over the data.

Which one finishes the pass sooner?
The big one · question 9

One epoch, 500,000 rows, every row seen once either way. Which finishes in less time?

The numbers

To time full batch at all we shrink the data to 500,000 rows, because at two million it will not run.

python
for batch_size in [1, 32, 128, 1024, 8192, N_ROWS]:
    steps = math.ceil(N_ROWS / batch_size)

    for _ in range(3):                   # warmup, not timed
        train_step(net, X, y, batch_size)

    torch.cuda.synchronize()             # wait for the GPU to actually finish
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for k in range(steps):               # one full pass over the data
        train_step(net, X, y, batch_size, offset=k * batch_size)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()             # again, or we time nothing at all

    print("batch %7d  %8d updates  %9.4f s per epoch"
          % (batch_size, steps, time.perf_counter() - t0))

output

batch     128     3,907 updates     0.4104 s per epoch
batch   1,024       489 updates     0.1885 s per epoch

Segment 5 / the measurement
Seconds for one pass over the data
One epoch means one pass over all 500,000 rows, whatever the batch size. Full batch does it in 0.1565 s with a single update. Stochastic gradient descent does it in 32.7 s, using 500,000 updates. That is a factor of 209, and it points the opposite way to almost everyone's intuition.

Why

Every step costs a fixed amount just to happen, whatever its size: the loop runs, work is handed to the GPU, the two sides wait for each other. Here that is about 65 microseconds. The actual arithmetic for one row is about 0.31 microseconds. So we pay 65 to do 0.31, two million times over.

Segment 5 / why the hardware sits idle
Where each step actually goes
Every step, whatever its size, pays the same fixed cost: the Python loop, the kernel launches, the synchronisation. On this hardware that cost is about 65 microseconds. At batch size 1 the useful arithmetic is 0.31 microseconds, so 99.5% of the step is pure overhead. At batch size 8,192 the same fixed cost is spread over 8,192 rows and almost disappears.
arithmetic the model needsfixed cost of asking for it
EVERY BAR IS ONE STEP, NORMALISED TO ITS OWN LENGTH

This is the whole explanation. A processor with thousands of parallel lanes is being handed one row at a time, and it spends 99.5% of its life waiting to be told what to do next. Batching is not about the maths, it is about giving the hardware enough work per instruction to be worth the instruction.

The middle

Memory pushes the batch size down, hardware pushes it up, so the answer is in between. A few hundred rows: big enough to keep the GPU busy, small enough that the activations are megabytes and not gigabytes.

python
BATCH = 128            # not 1, and not everything

for start in range(0, N_ROWS, BATCH):
    xb = X[start:start + BATCH]      # a small slice, not one row
    yb = y[start:start + BATCH]
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = ((net(xb).squeeze(1) - yb) ** 2).mean()   # averaged over 128 rows,
    loss.backward()                  # so the odd customers cancel each other
    opt.step()

Mini-batch gradient descent: a handful of rows per step
Each gradient is an average over a small random subset, so individual oddities partly cancel while the trend survives. It wobbles, but around the right direction.

Last two columns measured over the final 200 of 400 updates.

Noise is the price of a cheap gradient, and it is a price worth paying. The single sample run sits 22 times further from the minimum than full batch, but each of its updates costs 200 times less data. The right hand panel charges each run for the rows it actually touched, and on that axis the cheap noisy gradient reaches a decent answer first.
Segment 5 / the modern middle ground
Fits in memory, keeps the hardware busy, updates often enough
Three constraints, and only one option clears all of them at once. Full batch wins on speed and loses on memory. Stochastic wins on memory and loses badly on speed. Mini-batch gives up 2.6 times the epoch time of full batch and gets 3,906 times less memory and 3,907 updates in return.
fits in memoryupdates per epochwall clock per epochpath to the minimum
full batchno, needs 26.18 GB at 2,000,000 rows10.1565 s (fastest)smoothest
stochastic, batch 1trivially, 13.1 KB500,00032.7 s (slowest)jittery
mini-batch of 128easily, 1.7 MB3,9070.4104 smildly noisy

Memory column is judged at 2,000,000 rows, the size where full batch stops being possible. Timings are for 500,000 rows, the size where full batch still runs and can therefore be compared at all.

Mini-batch is not a compromise between two good options. It is the only option that fits in memory, keeps the hardware busy, and updates often enough to converge in a handful of passes instead of a few thousand. That is why every framework you will ever use defaults to it, and why batch_size=32 is the most copied line in machine learning.
Check yourself · question 10

Mini-batch is slower per epoch than full batch and noisier than full batch. So why is it the default everywhere?

The answer

A few hundred rows. Not one, and not all of them.

All of them is the correct gradient and the fastest pass, but it needs 26.18 GB and we have 14.7. One row at a time fits in kilobytes but is 209 times slower per pass, because a machine built for thousands of parallel lanes is being handed one row at a time. A few hundred clears all three constraints at once, which is why batch_size=32 is the most copied line in machine learning.

Segment 6

Where we got to

Five questions, five answers:

  1. Is one score enough? No. It gives height, not slope.
  2. What does the problem look like? A bowl, so downhill is obvious once you can see it. But you cannot usually see it.
  3. Is knowing the direction enough? No. A fixed step cannot be both accurate and quick.
  4. Is there something that already knows how far? Yes, the slope. Sign for direction, size for distance, and it fades out as you arrive.
  5. How big should the multiplier be, and how much data per step? Inside a narrow window, shrinking on a timetable, on a few hundred rows at a time.
The assumption underneath all of it

One thing to carry forward. Everything on this page rested on the surface being a bowl: one bottom, no surprises.

Next lecture

Everything today lived on a bowl with exactly one bottom. Real loss surfaces are not bowls. Next lecture: what breaks, and what momentum, RMSProp and Adam do about it.
